Mockup rev 3 · 26 August 2026

The project header

The facts moved to the left, and a third arrangement: one box, divided — owner, start and end down the left, brief and stakeholders as two rows on the right. Both are the real platform with the header block replaced in the running page.

What the Timeline box is for — and the honest answer is “almost nothing”

By date / By quarter records which form a project’s dates were planned in. It arrives on the import template and has been shown as a pill on the band ever since.

It used to decide how every date on the project was read. That stopped: either form is now right on any row, because a workshop lands on a day and a report lands in a month and one project has both. So the reader stopped asking.

Today it gates exactly one thing — whether the platform works out that a milestone finishes after the project ends (the pink note at the bottom of the page). And even that is nearly redundant: the calculation needs two real dates and gives up without them anyway. The only case where the flag changes anything is a project marked By quarter whose end date is a real date — where it suppresses a warning that would have been true.

So I have left it out of both proposals below. It is not a fact about the project that anybody acts on, and hiding a correct warning is a separate thing to decide — worth doing on its own rather than inside a header redesign.

Today— for comparison

Two headings and a paragraph, and the dates nowhere.

C, with the facts on the left— what you asked for

The same table, moved. It reads well and the eye lands on who and when before the prose — which is arguably the right order for a page you are scanning. The cost is that the brief now starts at an indent, so the pane has two left edges.

D, one divided box— three rows left, two rows right Recommended

One border, one ground, one hairline down the middle. Owner, start and end stack on the left; the brief and the stakeholders are two labelled rows on the right. It reads as one object — the project’s front matter — rather than as a table sitting next to some prose, and it is the shortest of the three: 127px against C’s 137px and a good deal less than today once the dates are added. It is also the only one where every label lines up in a column.

At 1000px— your laptop

Both stack, and both stay honest: every value on one line, nothing pushed outside the pane. D stays marginally shorter. Neither has the fault you spotted — the block is measured against the pane’s content box now, not against whether the page happens to scroll.

C left — 270px

D — 266px

What either one brings with it

  • The band keeps the code and the name and loses the rest. The owner moves into the block and the Timeline pill goes entirely. That is a visible change on every project page, so it is the part to look at twice.
  • The pen has to edit start and end. They arrive by upload today with no way to correct one on the page — a field nobody can fill is worse than no field.
  • Performance and Reporting should show the same block, read-only, or one project says different things depending which tab you are on.
  • Nothing new is stored. Owner, start, end and stakeholders all exist already.
  • It needs min-width: 0 wherever a table is involved, or the platform’s global 620px table minimum pushes it 300px past the pane. D avoids the trap entirely by not using a <table>.

Still a mockup

  • Nothing in the platform has changed. Say C left or D and I will build it — and say separately whether the Timeline flag should stop suppressing that overrun warning.
